title: The Art School
victoryHeadline: Caught! Call it her final piece.
acts: The end-of-term prize judging at the Academy had reduced everyone to their worst selves. In the Painting Studio, Everly — eighty if she was a day, silver hair down to her elbows, enrolled since the building had gas lamps — had planted herself directly south of her easel and refused to move, on the grounds that all great art is viewed from below, like a cathedral ceiling, or a very tall friend. Two easels over, Ginevra had done the unthinkable and sat down. Hers was the only occupied chair in the entire school, a fact she wore like a crown, blue fringe swept back, one hoop earring glinting with the smugness of the seated. "Standing is a stylistic choice," she informed the room. "I've chosen differently." Hartley, flat cap low, said nothing at all. He had spent forty minutes beside the long table mixing a single shade of ochre, and had reached the stage of the process where speaking to him was considered an act of vandalism.

Elsewhere the Academy conducted its usual dignified business. In the Office, Ben stood nose-to-varnish with the framed painting on his own wall — the school's one genuinely valuable canvas — moustache twitching, doing sums about insurance in a voice he believed was inaudible. On the Model Platform, Fritz held a magnificent, agonising, entirely unobserved pose on the carpet, jaw set, beard immaculate, for a life-drawing class that had abandoned him twenty minutes earlier to go and argue about the prize. He did not break the pose. Fritz has never broken a pose. Deep in Supplies, Anthony was alone by choice and by policy, wedged between a spare chair and a rack of easels, counting sable brushes against a clipboard and finding, as ever, that eleven were missing and that the culprit had left glitter. Down in the Gallery, Coralie stood guard at the plinths in her black vest, glaring at the statuary as though daring one of them to blink first.

The crash, when it came, was not a normal crash. It was architectural. It arrived from the far end of the building with a boom that shivered the ochre in Hartley's mixing dish, knocked Everly's easel a full degree off true, and did not so much as dislodge Fritz. It was followed by a strange snowfall of plaster dust that drifted through three rooms and settled, tastefully, on everything. Coralie got there first. Anthony arrived second, still holding the clipboard. What they found was, technically speaking, a new work: enormous, white, freshly settled, and — the assembled faculty were forced to agree — quite unlike anything Veronica had ever produced. Chiefly because Veronica was under it.

whereabouts.A: Anthony had barricaded himself in Supplies with a clipboard, auditing sable brushes between a spare chair and the easel rack, on the firm principle that people are worse than inventory.
whereabouts.B: Ben was in the Office, standing inches from the framed painting on his wall, muttering insurance valuations at it like a man reading a will.
whereabouts.C: Coralie was on patrol in the Gallery, planted beside a statue with her arms folded, staring down the marble in case any of it got ideas.
whereabouts.D: Delilah was in the Sculpting Studio in her cat-eye glasses, circling a colossal plaster piece with a chair to hand and the expression of a woman about to make one small, final, professional correction.
whereabouts.E: Everly had stationed herself on the floor of the Painting Studio directly south of her easel, painting upward on the theory that all masterpieces are best received from underneath.
whereabouts.F: Fritz was holding an unbroken life-drawing pose on the carpet of the Model Platform, entirely alone, for a class that had wandered off to argue about the prize.
whereabouts.G: Ginevra was in the Painting Studio committing the school's great heresy — sitting down, in the only occupied chair on the premises, and letting everybody know about it.
whereabouts.H: Hartley was beside the long table in the Painting Studio, forty minutes into mixing one shade of ochre and treating conversation as sabotage.
whereabouts.V: Veronica was in the Sculpting Studio, magenta hair and all, being talked at beside her prize-favourite piece by a colleague with strong feelings about the shortlist.

reveal: It was Delilah, in the Sculpting Studio, by means of a twelve-foot plaster figure and one exquisitely judged shove. Veronica's piece had been running away with the prize; Delilah's had been described in the student paper as "competent." So she steadied herself against the nearest chair, leaned in, and gave the great white sculpture the sort of corrective nudge one gives a wobbly bookcase — after which it toppled with the slow, inevitable, ceiling-shaking grandeur of a felled monument, and Veronica became, permanently, part of the composition. Delilah dusted the plaster off her sleeves, adjusted her glasses, stepped back, tilted her head, and pronounced it her strongest work to date.

escape.generic: The prize was quietly awarded to nobody, the plaster dust was swept into a bin bag marked ARCHIVE, and the real killer went right on accepting compliments on their recent work.

byAccused.A: Anthony was led away still clutching the clipboard, insisting that eleven missing sable brushes constituted the only crime committed on the premises that afternoon.
byAccused.B: Ben went along protesting that a man valuing his own framed painting is exhibiting prudence, not motive, and that the moustache was hereditary.
byAccused.C: Coralie was arrested for standing too near the statuary with a suspicious amount of enthusiasm, which she maintained was simply good invigilation.
byAccused.E: Everly was helped up off the floor and into a squad car, complaining that nobody had thought to take her statement from the correct angle.
byAccused.F: Fritz was taken in while still holding the pose, and by all accounts held it for the entire interview.
byAccused.G: Ginevra was hauled off mid-sit, protesting that being the only person in the school comfortable enough to use a chair is a matter of posture, not guilt.
byAccused.H: Hartley was marched out with his ochre unfinished, which he considered by some distance the greater injustice.
